title: Welcome to RIARS
keywords: RIARS, manual, overview, radio automation, help
text: RIARS stands for Renou Integral Automation Radio Solution. It is open-source radio automation with native support for AI agents. You can use it to run a station from a desktop computer, or headless from a server or Raspberry Pi. What RIARS does RIARS plays and manages your station: a media library that scans folders of audio files and searches them; a playlist with start times, item kinds, saved lists and generated items; playback with transport controls, volume, seek and crossfade; a silence detector that can skip a silent item or raise an alarm; streaming to an Icecast server in MP3; scheduled events for one-off or repeating actions; long-term automation: categories, format clocks, a dayparts grid and a generator that prepares what airs next; advertising with advertisers, campaigns, sponsorships and a delivery report; a proof-of-play log for billing and music reporting. The desktop app has the full graphical interface. The headless riars-server runs the same engine on a server and serves a small browser panel at http://YOUR-SERVER:3100/. AI agents can use the REST API or the MCP server. How to use this manual Each topic explains one job. Start with First steps to add music and get on air, then read The main window to learn where everything is. If you run a station without a screen, read Web panel and Headless server. Tip: press F1 in the desktop app to open this manual at any time. Where the desktop app and the browser panel differ, the topic says which one it means. Radio terms are explained in the Glossary.

title: First steps
keywords: start, add music, playlist, play, automation, quick start
text: This is the shortest path from an empty RIARS to a station that plays by itself. Add music to the library Open the desktop app and find the Library area on the left. Click Add folder and choose one or more folders of audio files, or tick them in the Folders tab. RIARS scans them in the background and adds the tracks to the library database; a message tells you how many new tracks were added. RIARS remembers these folders and rescans them every time it starts. Build a playlist Find a track in the library and double-click it. The track is added to the Playlist tab. Repeat for the first few songs. You can also search the library with the Search... box, and remove or reorder items in the playlist. Play Click Play in the transport controls at the top. The On air area shows the current track with its progress and time left; the right-hand Now Playing card shows the same information. Pause, Stop and Next work as you would expect. Turn on automation On the right, find the Automation card and click its toggle so it reads ON. In a new installation the generator has nothing to play yet: it needs at least a category, a clock and something in the grid. A simple setup: Open the Categories tab and click New. Give the category a name, choose the kind Music, save it, then add tracks to it. Open the Clocks tab. Create a clock with Add slot, choose the Fill type and pick your music category. Save the clock. Open the Grid tab and create a rule that plays that clock every day, all day. Save it. In Categories, open Station settings and choose the clock as Default clock. Save the settings. The generator now keeps a few items ahead of the air. It adds them to the end of the playlist and never cuts what is already playing. Read Automation overview for the whole picture, and Library and Playlist for the details.

title: The main window
keywords: window, layout, menus, on air bar, status bar, tabs
text: The desktop window is laid out like a broadcast console: what is on air first, then the tools, then the automation setup. Top of the window The header holds the RIARS logo, the transport controls (Play, Pause, Stop, Next and the Vol slider), the streaming badge and the language selector. Below it, the On air bar shows, from left to right: the date, the local time and the time left of the track on air; Previous, the track that just finished; On air, the current track, with a progress bar and its position and duration; Next, the track that will follow. Items that are not music show their kind next to the label, such as Jingle, Spot or Station ID. Left, centre and right The left sidebar contains the Library, with its Library and Folders tabs. The centre holds eight tabs: Playlist, Schedule, Clocks, Grid, Categories, Advertising, Log and Live (see Live broadcasting). Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+8 switch between them in that order. The right sidebar contains the Now Playing card, the VU Meter, the Log pane with recent proof-of-play entries and automation warnings, and the Automation card with its ON/OFF toggle. The bottom StatusBar shows the silence detector (Silence detector: on or off, or a red SILENCE ON AIR), the automation state (Automation: on or off), the number of active scheduled events and the RIARS version. Menus The in-window menu bar follows the RadioBOSS style: File: Add folder to library… · Open playlist… · Save playlist… · Export log (CSV)… · Quit Edit: Search the library · Clear the playlist View: the seven tabs · Language ▸ Playback: Play · Pause · Stop · Next · Crossfade… · Silence detector… · Normalisation… · Sound cards… Automation: Automation on/off · Preview… · Clocks · Grid · Categories · Advertising · Station settings Broadcast: Streaming settings… · Start streaming · Stop streaming Help: Manual (F1) · Keyboard shortcuts · Web panel and server · About RIARS The same actions are available from the tabs and cards described in this manual. See Playback and Automation overview. The browser panel has a different, smaller layout: see Web panel.

title: Media library
keywords: library, folders, folder tree, explorer, scanning, rescan, search, tracks, add music
text: The Library is the list of audio files RIARS knows about. The Library tab shows them in one searchable list; the Folders tab is a folder tree for choosing which folders the library is built from and for browsing their files. Add music The library is built from library folders. RIARS remembers them and rescans them every time it starts, so new music you copy into them shows up by itself. There are three ways to add folders: Folders tab: a tree of the computer that opens with ▸. Tick the box of each folder you want in the library; you can tick several in a row. Add folder, above the library, or File ▸ Add folder to the library… (Ctrl+Shift+A): the chooser lets you pick several folders at once. Add… in the Folders tab does the same. RIARS scans in the background, subfolders included, and the notice line says which folder it is reading and how many new tracks it found. You can keep working meanwhile. Rescanning only adds what is new: tracks already in the library are not duplicated and their tags are not read again. It reads MP3, FLAC, WAV, OGG, AAC and M4A files, taking title, artist, album, genre and duration from their tags; a file without tags uses its file name as the title. What is missing can be completed from MusicBrainz. On the headless server, --scan adds a library folder at startup, and the REST API and MCP server can list, add, remove and rescan library folders. The Folders tab At the top is the list of Library folders, with how many tracks each holds, and Rescan to look for new music without restarting. Below it is the tree of the computer: A ticked box is a library folder. A ticked but greyed box means the folder is already included through a folder higher up. When you untick a folder, or press ✕ in the list, RIARS asks whether to remove only the folder (its tracks stay) or its tracks too. Files are never deleted from disk. Clicking a folder's name lists its audio files underneath; double-clicking it also opens or closes it, like ▸. Files not yet in the library are dimmed, but you can still use them. Opening the Marks… of one of them from the playlist adds it to the library there and then, since marks are kept with the track. Files in that list work like library tracks: double-click or Enter adds them to the playlist, you can drag them onto the playlist or a sound bank button, and they have a right-click menu. Search Type in the Search... box. RIARS searches the library in the background shortly after you stop typing, matching title, artist, album and genre; every word must match, and case and accents are ignored. Clear the box to see the whole library again. Ctrl+L puts the cursor in the search box. The counter under the search box shows the number of matching tracks. The list loads in pages as you scroll, so a very large library does not have to load all at once. Add a track to the playlist Double-click a track, or press Enter, to add it to the Playlist. It goes at the end of the current list. You can then start it from the playlist, or let it wait its turn. You can select several tracks: Ctrl+click adds or removes one, Shift+click selects a range and Ctrl+A selects all. Right-click menu Right-click a track, or the selection: Option What it does Add to playlist At the end of the playlist. Play next Right after what is playing now. Pre-listen On the pre-listen card, not on air. Marks… Opens the intro and outro editor. Detect marks Analyses the chosen tracks; hand-set marks are kept. Complete metadata… Looks up the missing artist, album, year, genre and cover in MusicBrainz. See Complete metadata. Show in folder Shows the file in the file manager. Copy path Copies the file path. Remove from library… Asks first. The file stays on disk, but the track leaves its categories. Delete does the same. Tip: the library list is for choosing music. For the order of the show, use the Playlist tab. If a track will not play, RIARS reports Cannot play this file with the reason; check that the file still exists and that its format is supported. See First steps for a quick start.

title: Playlist
keywords: playlist, start time, reorder, save, open, generated, kinds, drag, drop, folder, explorer
text: The Playlist tab is the running order of the station. It shows what has played, what is on air and what comes next, including items the automation adds. What the columns mean Column Meaning # Position in the list Start Estimated start time, based on the position of the track on air Title Track title, with a coloured dot for its kind Artist Artist, or Unknown Album, Year and Genre The track's data in the library. A dash means the track is not in the library or lacks that field; Complete metadata can fill them in. Duration Length of the item The dot colour follows the item kind: music, Jingle, Bumper, Station ID, Sweeper, Promo, Spot, Programme, Music bed or Other. Hover over the dot to see the kind and whether the item was added by the automation. Start times move as the current track is seeked, paused or crossfaded. Reorder and edit Use the arrows on each row for Move up and Move down (or Alt+Up / Alt+Down), the cross for Remove (or Delete, also for several selected items), or Clear to empty the list. Double-click a row, or press Enter, to jump to it and start playing. Ctrl+click, Shift+click and Ctrl+A select several items. Right-click an item for: Play now, Play next, Pre-listen, Marks…, Move up, Move down, Move to top, Move to bottom, Remove from playlist, Remove played items, Clear the playlist, Show in folder and Copy path. Tabs: several lists at once There is a tab above the playlist for each open list, so you can prepare a programme's inserts in one tab while another plays. Only one list plays: the one with the red dot (on air). The others are edited the same way (dragging, right-click, marks) but play nothing: double-click and Enter pre-listen. + opens an empty list. Double-click a tab to rename it; ✕ closes it (asking first when it has items; save it first to keep it). The tab on air cannot be closed. Add to playlist in the library or Folders adds to the tab you are looking at. Play next always goes to the list on air. Starts at: the planned start time of a list that is not on air. The Start column counts from it, so you see when each item will play. Put on air (button, or right-click the tab): the track playing ends, then this list follows, with no cut. The list that was playing stays in its tab with what it had left, so putting it back on air carries on where it was. Right-click items: Copy to or Move to another tab and, from a list not on air, Insert next on air, right after the track playing. Tabs are saved with every change and come back when RIARS starts. Add by dragging You can build the playlist by dragging: From File Explorer (or your system's file manager): drag one or more audio files, or a whole folder, and drop them on the list. From the library, in its tracks and folders tabs: drag a track onto the list. While you drag, a red line shows where the items will go: above the row under the pointer or, in the lower half of the row, just below it. Drop below the last row to add them at the end. Near the top or bottom edge, the list scrolls by itself. Files go in in the order you drag them. A folder brings all its audio files, including those in its subfolders: first the folder's own files, by name, then each subfolder, also by name. Hidden and system folders are skipped, as in the library's folder tree. Anything that is not audio (pictures, text files…) is skipped. MP3, FLAC, WAV, OGG, AAC and M4A are supported. Files that are not in the library yet are added to it first and analysed in the background, so they get intros and outros and normalisation like the rest. With a big folder, the foot of the list shows the progress ("Adding to the library: 120 of 3000") and you can keep using the program. When it ends, it says how many were added and how many skipped. At most 10,000 files are added at once. Items added by the automation appear at the end. You can move or remove them; the generator respects what you leave and only fills the end of the list. It does not rewrite the items already there. Save and open Click Save, type a Playlist name and confirm: it saves the list of the tab you are looking at. Open opens a saved playlist in a new tab, leaving the list on air alone; the list shows their name, number of items and total duration, and a cross deletes them. Saved playlists can also be used as a source in clocks and grid rules. Ctrl+S saves the current playlist and Ctrl+O opens a saved one. Length The footer shows the number of items and the total duration. A dash (--:--) means the duration is not known yet. Note: changing the playlist while the automation is on is allowed. The generator will fill the new end of the list on its next pass. See Automation overview and Playback.

title: Playback
keywords: play, pause, stop, next, volume, seek, keyboard
text: Playback controls are in the header and in the Now Playing card. They work the same whether a person or the automation loaded the track. Transport Play starts or resumes the current item. Pause holds it at the current position; Play resumes. Stop stops playback and resets the position. Next jumps to the next item in the playlist. The On air bar calls the current item On air, or Paused when paused. The Now Playing card shows ON AIR, PAUSED or STOPPED, the track title and a progress bar. Volume and seek Drag the Vol slider to set the output level; the percentage is shown next to it. The setting is saved with the session and restored on the next start unless the server started with --no-resume. To seek, click anywhere on the progress bar in Now Playing. RIARS moves the playhead to that point and keeps playing. The bar is only active when a track with a known duration is loaded. Keyboard In the desktop app: F5 Play, F6 Pause, F7 Stop, F8 Next track. Ctrl+Q quits. The full list is in Keyboard shortcuts. What happens at the end of a track By default the engine plays items in order. At the end of the list it stops, unless the automation is adding more items or you turned on repeat-by-hand. Before an item ends, the next one is prepared so the change is immediate; with crossfade on, the two overlap. Seamless changes are covered in Crossfade. Tip: if the station falls silent while an item is playing, the Silence detector may skip it. See Silence detector.

title: Crossfade
keywords: crossfade, fade, curve, overlap, spot, no overlap
text: Crossfade makes one item fade out while the next fades in. RIARS uses it to join tracks smoothly instead of leaving a hard cut or a gap. Defaults Crossfade is on by default, lasts 3 seconds and uses the Equal Power curve. You can change the length, choose a curve and turn it off from Playback › Crossfade… in the desktop menu. The same settings are available through the API. The three curves are: Curve Character Linear Simple, even fade; good for similar material Equal Power Keeps the perceived loudness steady through the join S-Curve Gentle start and end; a smooth, musical transition Spots and other protected kinds By default, Spot items never crossfade: a commercial starts and ends cleanly, without overlapping the music or the next spot. This is the Kinds that never crossfade setting in Station settings; you can add other kinds there, for example Station ID or Jingle. The generator marks each item according to that setting, and the audio engine skips the fade on both sides of it. This is why ad breaks sound separated from the music. Where the time comes from The start times in the Playlist and the length of a generated hour take the crossfade into account. If you change the crossfade length, the plan for the next items follows the new value. Note: a crossfade is not a fix for very different levels. Set the volume and the item's own audio sensibly; the VU Meter warns with CLIP if the output reaches full scale. See Station settings for the no-overlap kinds, and Silence detector for what happens when an item contains silence.

title: Silence detector
keywords: silence, dead air, detector, threshold, skip, alert
text: The silence detector watches the output while a track is playing. If the signal stays below a level for too long, it reports dead air and can skip the item. It protects the station when a file is empty, corrupt or has a long silent lead. Defaults Setting Default Enabled Yes Threshold -50 dBFS Length 10 seconds Action Skip The level is measured before the volume control, so turning the studio monitors down does not count as silence. It is reset by sound or by stopping playback. What you see When silence passes the limit, the Now Playing card shows a red SILENCE badge and the bottom bar changes to SILENCE ON AIR. The badge tooltip gives the number of incidents since the engine started. In the browser panel, the header shows SILENCE and the automation log may show a warning. With the Skip action, RIARS jumps to the next playlist item and marks the skipped item with the reason cut for silence in the proof-of-play log. With Alert, it only raises the alarm and keeps playing. Configure it In the desktop app, open Playback › Silence detector…. In the API, use GET and POST /api/v1/player/dead-air with enabled, thresholddb (from -90 to 0), seconds (1 to 600) and action (Skip or Alert). The MCP tool setdead_air exposes the same fields. Tip: if music with very quiet passages triggers false alarms, lower the threshold (for example to -60 dBFS) or lengthen the time. Do not disable the detector on an unattended station. See Playback and Troubleshooting.

title: Streaming
keywords: streaming, Icecast, SHOUTcast, MP3, bitrate, metadata, mount
text: RIARS can send the output of the station to an Icecast server as an MP3 stream. Listeners then connect to the Icecast server, not to RIARS directly. The desktop app needs an audio output device. The headless server can run on its internal clock with --no-sound-card, and streaming still works because RIARS encodes the mixed output; see Headless server. Configure and connect In the desktop app, click the streaming badge or use Broadcast › Streaming settings…. In the browser panel of riars-server, use the stream badge. Fill in: Field Meaning Server Icecast host name or IP address Port Icecast port, usually 8000 Mount point Stream path, for example /stream Bitrate 64, 96, 128, 160, 192, 256 or 320 kbps User and Password Icecast source credentials Station name and Genre Information sent to the server The defaults are localhost, port 8000, mount /stream, user source, 128 kbps and station name RIARS. The format is MP3. Click Connect to start; the badge shows CONNECTING, then STREAMING. Disconnect stops the stream. Status and metadata The badge can also show OFFLINE, STREAM ERROR or NO AUDIO. When connected, the panel shows the URL and the amount of data sent. The current song title is sent to Icecast automatically as Artist - Title when the track changes, and is sent again after a reconnection. The password is not saved between sessions; the other settings are remembered. Notes RIARS reconnects on its own if the connection drops. A mount point can only have one source at a time. If Icecast refuses the mount, another encoder may be using it. On the server, streaming settings can be resumed from the saved session unless it started with --no-resume. See Web panel for remote control and Troubleshooting if the stream will not connect.

title: Loudness normalisation
keywords: normalise, normalize, volume, loudness, lufs, ebu r128, level, replaygain, limiter
text: Every file is mastered at a different level: a recent song sounds much louder than one from the 80s, and a jingle can be very quiet. Normalisation evens out the perceived loudness so listeners do not have to reach for the volume. How it works The analysis measures each track's integrated loudness to the EBU R128 standard (in LUFS) and its peak. It is the same pass that finds intros and outros, and it is done once per track. On air, each track gets one fixed gain to reach the target: −16 LUFS by default, usual for Internet radio. A quiet track is raised only as far as its peak allows, and never more than the limit. A soft limiter on the output prevents clipping when something was raised or when a jingle plays over a song. Tracks that were not raised pass untouched. A track that has not been analysed uses its ReplayGain tags, when it has them and the option is ticked. Otherwise it plays as it is. Settings Playback ▸ Normalisation… Setting Default Enabled Yes Target −16 LUFS Most gain 10 dB Most cut 12 dB Peak ceiling −1 dBFS Target for spots The same (empty) Target for jingles and IDs The same (empty) Use ReplayGain tags for tracks not analysed yet Yes The two own targets let spots or station imaging play slightly above or below the music: for example, spots at −15 LUFS with music at −16. Leave them empty to use the general target. The LUFS column of the playlist shows each track's loudness. The cue-point editor shows the gain the track will get. Tip: analyse the whole library once (Categories ▸ Track analysis ▸ Analyse library). Whatever you add later can be analysed with the same button; it only processes what is new.

title: Sound cards and pre-listening
keywords: sound card, output, device, pre-listen, cue, pfl, headphones, listen
text: RIARS can use two sound cards: one for on air (what the station sends out) and one for pre-listening (hearing something on headphones without it going on air). Choosing them Playback ▸ Sound cards… On air: the card the broadcast goes out on. By default, the system one. The change applies when RIARS restarts, so the broadcast is not cut. Pre-listen: the headphones card, or Off. It applies at once. Warning: if you choose the on-air card for pre-listening too, what you listen to will be heard on air. The dialog warns you in yellow. Pre-listening has its own audio engine, separate from the on-air one: a failure in it cannot affect the broadcast. If the pre-listen card goes away, for example when USB headphones are unplugged, it simply stops playing. Pre-listening In the library: right-click a track ▸ Pre-listen. In the cue-point editor: the ▶ buttons play the start, the end of the intro or the end of the voice. Pre-listening plays at the level the track would have on air, with normalisation applied. On the headless server riars-server --list-devices lists the sound cards, and --device "<name>" chooses the on-air one. The server has no pre-listening. See Headless server.

title: Live broadcasting
keywords: live, microphone, mic, sound bank, cartwall, jingles, effects, manual mode, assisted, on air, presenter, DJ, echo, direct monitoring
text: The On air tab (Ctrl+8) brings together what a presenter needs: the microphone, the sound bank and the mode the playlist moves on in. Microphone The MIC button (or F9 from any tab) opens and closes it, with a short fade so no click is heard. While it is open the button turns red and ON AIR shows. When it opens, the music goes down by itself (12 dB by default) and comes back when it closes. To lower it only while you speak, choose While speaking in the settings. The meter shows the level even with the microphone closed, so you can check your voice before going on air. Keep the peaks in the green or yellow. If the microphone's card fails or is unplugged, the microphone falls silent and the error shows in red. The broadcast goes on. Playback ▸ Microphone… (or the ⚙ button): Setting Default Input card The system one The sound card already plays the microphone (direct monitoring) No Gain 0 dB Low cut (removes pops and hum below 80 Hz) Yes Noise gate (silences room noise between phrases) No Compressor (evens out loud and quiet speech) Yes Lower the music 12 dB, while open Let the API and AI agents open it No RIARS does not send the microphone to the pre-listen headphones: to hear yourself, use the mixing desk or your audio interface's direct monitoring. If you hear an echo Many audio interfaces (a Roland UA-4FX, for example) send the microphone input straight to their output, with no delay. If RIARS plays it on that card as well, you hear yourself twice: the second copy arrives a fraction of a second late and sounds like an echo. If the card output is your on-air signal, listeners hear it too. Tick The sound card already plays the microphone (direct monitoring). RIARS then stops playing the microphone on the card, which already does so with no delay, and adds it only to the Internet stream. The music still ducks when the microphone opens and the meter still works. If your interface has no direct monitoring, leave the box unticked; otherwise the microphone would not reach the card at all. Sound bank A grid of 6 × 4 buttons with 8 pages, for jingles, effects, sweepers and music beds. You can keep several banks, one per show for example, and pick the active one at the top. Assign a sound: drag a track from the library (or a file from the Folders tab) onto a button, or click an empty button. In the editor, clicking Choose a track… shows the library list, which filters as you type; Choose file… takes any audio file on disk, in the library or not. Fire: click the button, or keys 1–0 and Q–P for the first twenty buttons of the visible page. Page Up / Page Down change page. Esc or Stop all stops every bank sound. Each button shows the time it has left while it plays. Up to 8 can play at once, over the music, and with the playlist stopped too. Right-click a button: Edit… (label, colour, gain, mode and whether it lowers the music), Pre-listen and Clear. Button mode What it does Fire Every press starts it from the top. Toggle One press starts it, the next stops it. Loop It repeats until you stop it. Handy for music beds. Short sounds (under 30 s) are loaded into memory when their page opens, so they play at once. Everything played from the bank goes into the proof-of-play log. Playlist mode Mode What it does Automatic The playlist moves on by itself and the automation fills it. Assisted The playlist moves on by itself, but the automation adds nothing and makes no cuts: what you prepared plays. Manual When each item ends the playlist stops and waits for Play (F5) or Next (F8). In any mode, right-click ▸ Stop after this item in the playlist stops the broadcast when that item ends. Handy to come in and talk. The item shows ⏹. Talking over the intro When a song with intro marks starts, the panel shows in green the seconds left before the voice comes in; the last three in yellow. You can introduce the song and stop talking just in time.

title: Complete metadata
keywords: metadata, tags, artist, album, year, genre, cover, artwork, musicbrainz, acoustid, fingerprint, identify, complete
text: RIARS can look up what your library tracks are missing in open catalogues: title, artist, album, year, genre and cover. Looking up changes nothing. You see what was found next to what each track has, and only what you tick is applied. Filling in year and genre also helps automation: smart categories can filter by them. Opening it There are two ways to open it. Neither starts on its own: the top of the dialog says what will be looked up, and the lookup starts when you press Look up. Right-click ▸ Complete metadata… in the library looks up the selected tracks, even if they already have every field. Use it to check a particular track. Edit ▸ Complete library metadata… looks up the tracks of a minute or longer that have a gap (no artist, album, genre or year). Shorter ones, such as jingles and station IDs, are skipped because no catalogue lists them; the dialog says how many. To look one of them up, select it and use the right-click menu. When Look up can't be pressed, the reason is shown next to it: There is nothing to look up: no track is missing anything. A lookup is running: only one can run at a time. Wait for it to finish or press Stop. The lookup runs in the background. You can close the dialog and open it again to see how it is going. Stop ends it after the current track and keeps what was found. Where the data comes from MusicBrainz is an open music encyclopedia whose data is public domain (CC0). RIARS searches for the recording by the title and artist in the tags and compares the length. If a track has no tags but the file is named "Artist - Title", it searches by the name. AcoustID is optional. It recognises a song by how it sounds (its audio fingerprint), even when the file has no tags at all. It needs an application key, entered at the top of the dialog and kept with the library. It is free for non-commercial use: register one at acoustid.org/new-application. A commercial station needs its own key from acoustid.biz. Cover Art Archive supplies the album cover. MusicBrainz allows one request per second, so each track takes 2 to 4 seconds: about 500 tracks take about 20 minutes. When the same song is on several releases (the original, a live album, a compilation), RIARS prefers the album the track already names. Otherwise it takes the earliest studio album. Review and apply Each track found shows the cover, how it was found (by tags, by file name or by fingerprint) and the confidence. Below that is every field that would change, with the current value → the new one. Only the gaps start ticked: empty fields, or a title that is just the file name. What a track already has is never ticked for you; tick it yourself to change it. Apply stores what is ticked in the library. Each track records where its data came from (musicbrainz: and the recording's identifier). Also write the tags into the audio files is off by default. It also saves the values and the cover inside the file, so other programs see them, and asks first. RIARS writes a copy, checks that it reads back, and only then replaces the original. A file that is playing may not be replaceable, and RIARS says so. Covers are kept in the riars_covers folder next to the library database. Tracks with no match are listed at the end, folded, with the reason when there was an error (for example, no connection). For agents and the API The REST API has POST /api/v1/library/metadata/lookup to start, GET on the same path for the status and proposals, POST /library/metadata/apply, and /library/metadata/settings for the key. The MCP server offers lookuptrackmetadata, metadatalookupstatus, applytrackmetadata, gettrackmetadata and setacoustidkey. See API and agents.

title: RDS
keywords: rds, radiotext, rt, rt+, ps, pi, pty, encoder, uecp, fm, station name, serial port, mpx, stereo encoder, pilot, pre-emphasis, 192 khz

title: Scheduled events
keywords: schedule, event, once, daily, weekly, interval, action
text: The Schedule tab (the Scheduling section of the manual) runs simple actions at fixed times. It is separate from the long-term automation: events do something once, or on a repeating pattern, while the grid decides what airs hour by hour. Event types When Meaning Once The next time that time comes; the event then disables itself Every day The same time every day Every week A weekday and time Every N minutes A repeating interval Each event has a Name. The list shows its When and its Action, a checkbox to enable or disable it and a cross to remove it. A disabled event stays in the list but does not run. Actions Action What it does Play track Plays a chosen file immediately Play playlist Loads and plays a saved playlist Set volume Sets the output level Fade volume Fades to a level over a number of Seconds Start streaming Starts the Icecast connection Stop streaming Stops it To add an event, fill in Name, When, the time or Minutes, and Action, then click Add. For Play track, use Choose file…; for Play playlist, choose a saved Playlist. Precision and saving Events run with second precision. One-off events disable themselves after firing, so they do not repeat the next day. The schedule is saved as riars_schedule.json next to the library database in the data folder; it is loaded at startup by both the desktop app and riars-server. The bottom bar shows Event scheduler: N events. Tip: use a scheduled event for a daily news feed or a volume change, and the Grid for the normal music programming. For the difference between the two systems, see Automation overview.

title: Automation overview
keywords: automation, generator, categories, clocks, grid, ahead, warnings
text: Long-term automation lets RIARS program the station for days or weeks without an operator. It has four parts that fit together: Categories group the music and other audio the generator may choose. Format clocks describe what one hour sounds like: songs, jingles, station IDs and ad breaks. The grid decides which clock or saved playlist plays in each hour of the week, with exceptions by date. The generator picks the actual items and adds them to the end of the on-air playlist. All of this is stored in the library database. The schedule of events is separate and lives in riars_schedule.json; see Scheduled events. Turning it on In the desktop app, click the Automation card toggle so it reads ON, use Automation › Automation on/off, or press Ctrl+E. In the browser panel, use the automation toggle. Turning automation on or off does not cut what is playing: the generator starts adding items behind the current one. Turning it off leaves the current playlist alone. The card shows the Clock or Playlist being prepared, the Generating period (HH:MM–HH:MM) and the Grid rule. Warnings appear in yellow and in the Log pane. Generating ahead The generator works ahead of the air, so there is always something ready to play. By default it keeps at least 3 items and 15 minutes of audio in front of the current item (adjustable in Station settings). It runs when the current track changes or when the amount ahead falls below that horizon. It does not rewrite items already in the playlist; changes to categories, clocks, the grid or campaigns apply from the next generated item. If a category is empty it uses the Fallback category. If there is still nothing, it warns rather than leaving the station silent. The pieces Categories: kinds, subcategories, smart filters, weights, separation. Format clocks: slots and anchors. The grid: days, hours and exceptions. Preview: what would air. Station settings: defaults for the whole station.

title: Categories
keywords: category, subcategory, smart, filter, weight, separation, rules, codes
text: A Category is a group of tracks the generator can choose from: a music style, jingles, station IDs, spots or a programme. Open the Categories tab to create and edit them. Creating a category Click New, then fill in the Category editor: Field Meaning Name What you see in clocks and rules Kind Music, Jingle, Bumper, Station ID, Sweeper, Promo, Spot, Programme, Music bed or Other Colour Used in the list and in the clock pie Parent Makes this a subcategory of another category A clock that asks for a parent also draws from its children. Click Save to keep the category. Smart categories Tick Smart category (filter instead of assigned tracks) to let a filter choose the tracks at generation time. You can filter by Genre, Artist, Folder starts with, Year from and Year to, Energy min (0-5) and Energy max (0-5), and Min duration / Max duration in seconds. This is useful when the library is large: you do not have to assign every track by hand. Tracks and weights For a normal category, first save it, then choose a Weight (0.01-100) and use the track picker (Search the library) to add tracks. The table lists Title, Artist, Length, Weight and Last played; select rows and use Remove selected to take them out. A weight above 1 makes a track more likely to be picked; a weight below 1 makes it less likely. Separation Tick Own separation rules to override the station defaults for this category. Same song (minutes), Same artist (minutes) and Same album (minutes) set the minimum distance between repeats; Imaging between others sets how many other imaging items must pass before the same one can repeat; Horizontal separation avoids playing a track in the same hour as the previous day. The station defaults are 240 minutes for the same song and 45 minutes for the same artist. Auto-assignment rules Rules assign scanned tracks to this category automatically. Choose a Field (Genre, Artist or Folder), enter a Pattern, click Add rule, and later Apply rules now. Text matching ignores case and accents; for Folder the pattern is a prefix of the file path. Codes Codes are free labels on a track, such as lento, femenina, navidad or explícita. Clock slots can Require codes or Exclude codes, for example pop without explícita. Codes are managed through the API or MCP today. See Format clocks for using categories in a clock, and Station settings for the defaults.

title: Format clocks
keywords: clock, hour, slot, anchor, hard, soft, max wait, fill, pie
text: A Format clock describes what a period sounds like: one hour by default, or another Length (min) from 5 to 1440. It is a list of slots, some at fixed times (anchors) and some that simply follow the previous one. The Clocks tab On the left is the list of clocks with their colour and length; use New and Delete. The editor has Name, Colour, Length (min) and Fill category, then the Slots table with Time, Type, Details and Actions. Click Add slot to add one, Save to keep the clock and Discard to undo unsaved changes. The pie on the right shows how the period is divided. Slot types Type Use Category A number of tracks from a category; set Count and optionally Require codes / Exclude codes Imaging One jingle, sweeper, bumper or station ID from an imaging category Ad break A block filled with spots; set its Name, Max seconds, Intro category and Outro category Playlist A saved playlist, whole or the next Count items; blank means All Track A fixed file, for example a programme theme Fill Music from a category until the next anchor or the end of the clock Anchors Put a time in the Time column as mm:ss to make a slot an anchor: for example 15:00 for the ad break at a quarter past, or 00:00 for a station ID at the top of the hour. Leave it empty for a slot that follows the previous one. Anchors are soft by default: the block starts when the song playing at that time ends, so music is never cut. Max wait (s) limits how late a soft anchor may run. Tick Hard to cut in at the exact time; use it when you must join a network news bulletin. Hard anchors more than a minute late are dropped, for example after the machine has slept. Fixing the length Between anchors the generator places the unordered slots and uses Fill to reach the next anchor or the end. The Fill category on the clock is a second-level fallback when the slots run out. Use a Fill slot for music that must stop at the next fixed point, and the clock-level Fill category as a safety net. The hour pie The pie is a quick visual check: each slot gets a colour, and its size follows the planned duration. Gaps or an over-full hour show up immediately. See The grid to decide when this clock plays, and Station imaging for the jingles and IDs inside it.

title: The grid
keywords: grid, daypart, rule, priority, days, months, weeks, dates, exceptions, week view
text: The Grid decides which clock or saved playlist plays at each moment. It is a set of rules, shown over a normal week of 7 × 24 hours. Each coloured cell belongs to the rule that wins for that hour; the colour is the clock's colour, or blue for a playlist. Hours with no rule show the Default clock, or a dash if there is none. The week view Use the week arrows (Previous week and Next week) or the date box to move around. Click a coloured cell to select its rule and edit it below. Hover over a cell to see the rule name, its priority and what it plays. Above the week there is a strip with the days of the month. Outlined days have a rule with dates (From / To), that is, an exception: hover to see which one. Click a day to see its week. Creating a rule Click New, then fill in: Field Meaning Name A label for the rule Priority Higher wins when rules overlap Plays Choose Clock or Playlist, then the item itself Start and End Daily time span From and To Optional date range Enabled Whether the rule applies Days Monday to Sunday checkboxes Months January to December checkboxes Weeks of the month 1st to 5th, and Last The hint in the editor is important: Start equal to end means all day; end before start crosses midnight. A rule from 22:00 to 02:00 covers the late show across midnight. Click Save to store the rule. Delete removes it, and New starts a fresh one. Priority and exceptions For a given moment, the enabled rule with the highest Priority wins. If two rules have the same priority, the more specific one wins. A date-limited rule with a high priority is the usual way to make an exception, for example a Christmas clock on 25 December, or a summer schedule in July and August. If no rule applies, the Default clock from Station settings is used. If that is empty too, the automation adds nothing and the current playlist simply continues. Resolution by hour The grid is resolved at the start of each clock period. A 60-minute clock fills the hour; a 30-minute clock repeats twice. When a rule changes, the generator applies it from the next item it builds, so what is already on air is not cut. See Format clocks for what the rules play and Preview to check the result.

title: Station imaging
keywords: imaging, jingle, sweeper, bumper, station ID, intro, outro, ad break
text: Imaging is the short audio that gives the station its sound: jingles, sweepers, bumpers, station IDs and the music beds under a voice. In RIARS, imaging is organised as categories with an imaging Kind and placed in clocks or added by the generator's own rules. Jingles every N songs In Station settings, choose a Jingle category and a number in Jingle every N songs (0 = never). With, say, 3, the generator puts one jingle from that category after every three songs. Set it to None or 0 to stop this. Sweepers on a style change The Sweeper category on style change setting adds a sweeper between two songs when their categories differ. It is a way to smooth the change from, for example, pop to rock. If no category is chosen, no sweeper is added. Station IDs A station ID (audio logo) is an imaging element with the kind Station ID. Put it in a clock as an Imaging slot with a Time anchor of 00:00 to place it at the top of the hour. A Hard anchor cuts in at the exact second; a soft anchor waits for the current song to finish. A category can also include IDs, but the Imaging slot is the clear way to reserve one. Ad break frames An Ad break slot can have an Intro category and an Outro category. When the break has spots, RIARS plays an item from the intro category before the spots and one from the outro category after them. Leave them empty for a bare break. The maximum length is set in Max seconds, and the station default is 180 seconds. Making the categories Create categories with the right Kind for each purpose, for example Jingle, Sweeper, Bumper and Station ID, and add the files to them. The kind affects the colour in the playlist, the imaging rules and the no-overlap setting. Tip: keep imaging short and separate from music categories. Mixing them makes separation and the "every N songs" count unreliable. See Station settings for the imaging fields and Format clocks for placing imaging in an hour.

title: Station settings
keywords: settings, default clock, fallback, separation, ahead, ad break, no overlap
text: Station settings apply to the whole automation. In the desktop app they are at the bottom of the Categories tab: open the Station settings section. The same dialog is available from Automation › Station settings. Click Save settings when you are done. Main settings Field Meaning Automation enabled Same switch as the Automation card Default clock The clock used for hours no grid rule covers Fallback category Music used when a category has nothing playable Items ahead Minimum number of items the generator keeps in front of the air Minutes ahead Minimum amount of audio it keeps in front Keep played items How many finished items stay in the on-air playlist Keep the play log (months) Older proof-of-play lines are deleted at start and once a day; 0 keeps them all (default 13) Ad break seconds Default length of an ad break when the slot does not set one The defaults are 3 items and 15 minutes ahead, 20 played items kept and 180 seconds for an ad break. A larger horizon gives more warning of what comes next but corrects changes later. Default separation These values apply to categories that do not have Own separation rules: Field Default Same song (minutes) 240 Same artist (minutes) 45 Same album (minutes) 0 Imaging between others 3 Horizontal separation Off Zero disables a separation rule. If strict rules leave a small category with no candidate, the generator relaxes them rather than leaving silence, and writes a warning. Imaging Jingle category, Jingle every N songs (0 = never) and Sweeper category on style change control the automatic imaging. See Station imaging. Kinds that never crossfade This list decides which item kinds are protected from the crossfade. By default only Spot is in it, so commercials start and end cleanly. Tick other kinds, such as Station ID or Jingle, if they must not overlap music. Note: changes apply from the next item the generator builds. Items already in the playlist keep the settings they were generated with. See Categories and Automation overview.

title: Preview
keywords: preview, what would air, plan, difference, hours
text: Preview shows what the automation would put on air, without touching the playlist. Use it to check a new clock, a grid exception or an ad campaign before it runs. Where to find it In the desktop app, choose Automation › Preview…. The preview can cover up to 48 hours. In the browser panel, the Coming up list shows the next hour, with time, kind and title. In the API, use GET /api/v1/automation/preview?from=YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS&hours=N; the MCP tool is preview_schedule. The preview works whether automation is on or off, because it only asks the generator what it would choose. It writes nothing to the playlist or the log. Why it can differ from the air The preview is a plan, not a promise. It can differ from what finally airs because: the generator makes random choices among suitable tracks, and the real run has its own history; separation depends on what has actually played, including manual plays and skips; the operator can move, remove or add items, and the generator respects those edits; a hard anchor may cut in at the exact time, while a soft anchor waits for the current song; campaign pacing changes as spots air or are missed; settings or clocks changed after the preview was made apply to the next generated item. The browser panel says it plainly: Preview only. The Playlist card shows what is really on air. Tip: preview after saving a clock or a rule, not before, so the preview uses the values that will really be used. See Automation overview and The grid.

title: Intros, outros and talking over the intro
keywords: intro, outro, talk over, voice, marks, cue, cue points, jingle over, ducking, analysis
text: Radio stations often talk over the intro: a jingle or station ID plays over the instrumental start of a song and ends just before the singing begins. RIARS does this on its own, and never over the voice. The marks of each song Mark Meaning Cue in First moment with sound (leading silence skipped). Voice starts End of the instrumental intro. Voice ends Start of the instrumental outro. Cue out Last moment with sound. The Intro and Outro columns of the playlist show how many seconds can be talked over at the start and at the end. Detecting them One song: the ✎ button in the library, or right-click ▸ Marks…. The editor opens with the waveform. The whole library or a category: in Categories, the Track analysis box, button Analyse library or Analyse this category. It runs in the background, one song after another with pauses, so on-air playback keeps its CPU. Each song is analysed only once. Detection looks for the voice by its energy in the vocal band, the rhythm of syllables and its tone. It is approximate: it suggests, and you confirm or correct. Each automatic mark has a confidence value; below the minimum (0.35 by default) it is not used for talking over. Correcting them by hand In the editor: Drag the marks on the waveform or type the times. The arrow keys move a mark 0.1 s; Shift + arrows, 1 s. The coloured strip below shows, second by second, how much it sounds like a voice. Listen on the pre-listen card: ▶ Last 5 s of intro checks that the mark falls just before the voice. Press Save. Hand-set marks are never replaced by a later analysis. If the song has no intro, tick No intro. Detection with an AI agent In the Track analysis box you can choose another detector: External program: a program that separates the voice with AI (for example Demucs or Spleeter with a small script). RIARS passes it each file and reads the result. It is more accurate but uses more computer power. A program that takes longer than two minutes on one file is stopped. For safety it can only be chosen in the desktop app; the API refuses it. Agent over MCP: an agent such as Claude can review the doubtful songs with listtracksneedingreview, read the voice line of each one with analyzetrack and set the marks with settrackcues. They are saved with source Agent. An agent cannot replace marks you set by hand. See API and AI agents. How the automation talks over In Station settings ▸ Talk over intros and outros: Setting Default Enabled, over intros, over outros Yes Margin before the voice 500 ms Lower the song (ducking) 6 dB Minimum confidence of automatic marks 0.35 Kinds that may talk over Jingle, station ID, sweeper, bumper When a jingle is due, RIARS looks at the next song. If the whole jingle fits in the intro with the margin, it plays over it, placed to end just before the voice. While it plays, the song is lowered a few dB: quickly on the way in and gently on the way out. If it does not fit, it tries the outro of the previous song. If that does not fit either, it plays before the song, as usual. Spots never talk over, and neither do hard fixed times. What was played over is in the proof-of-play log with its real time.

title: Advertisers and campaigns
keywords: advertising, advertiser, campaign, spots per day, dayparts, max per hour, priority, rotation
text: The Advertising tab has three sub-tabs: Advertisers, Campaigns and Delivery. An advertiser is the company that buys airtime; a campaign is one agreement with dates, a daily target, allowed times and a set of spots. Advertisers Click New, fill in Name, Contact and Notes, and click Save. Delete removes the advertiser. You need at least one advertiser before you can create a campaign. Campaigns Choose an advertiser filter or All advertisers, then click New. In the Campaign editor: Field Meaning Advertiser Who the campaign belongs to Name Campaign name From and To First and last day it may air Spots per day Daily target; 0 means a pure sponsorship Max per hour (0 = no limit) Ceiling inside one clock hour Priority Higher goes first when a break is full On Enables or disables the campaign Under Dayparts, add the times when the campaign may air. Each daypart has Days, Start and End. No dayparts means any time. Use Add daypart and Remove daypart to build the allowed windows. Under Spots, use the track picker to add the audio. The table shows Title, Length and Weight; the weight controls how often each spot of the campaign is used. Save stores the campaign and Delete removes it. How spots are spread The traffic system divides the day into five-minute slices and compares what each campaign has aired with an even pace inside its dayparts. A campaign that is behind gets into the next suitable ad break, first by priority and then by how far behind it is. It may run at most about half a spot ahead of pace. Two spots from the same advertiser do not share a break, and the break's maximum length is respected. Spots never crossfade by default. See Sponsorships and Delivery report.

title: Sponsorships
keywords: sponsorship, programme, opening, closing, clock, grid rule
text: A sponsorship is a campaign that is linked to a programme or a time span instead of being spread through ordinary ad breaks. It plays a sponsor message at the Opening and/or the Closing of the programme: “This programme comes to you thanks to…”. Setting one up In the Advertising tab, open Campaigns and select or create a campaign. In the Sponsorship section choose: Field Meaning None No sponsorship Clock Sponsor every period of a clock; choose the Clock Grid rule Sponsor the span of a grid rule; choose the Grid rule Then tick Opening and/or Closing. The spots of the campaign are the messages that play; add them under Spots like any other campaign. A sponsorship does not need a daily spot target: Spots per day can be 0 when the campaign exists only to sponsor a programme. How it airs When the sponsored clock or rule starts, RIARS plays the opening spot before the first song. At the end of the period it plays the closing spot. If the same programme continues into the next hour, the sponsorship is not repeated, so the opening is heard once at the real start of the programme. What it is not A sponsorship is not an Ad break slot in a clock. Ad breaks are filled by the traffic system from all eligible campaigns; a sponsorship is fixed to its programme. You can use both in the same station: a sponsored morning show with its own clock, and ordinary breaks at :15 and :45. Tip: keep the sponsor message short and distinct from the programme audio. The proof-of-play log records it with the campaign, so the delivery report counts it. See Advertisers and campaigns and Delivery report.

title: Delivery report
keywords: delivery, report, missed spots, CSV, billing, campaign, aired, cut
text: The Delivery sub-tab of Advertising shows how each campaign did. It is the report you use to check a contract and to prepare billing. Reading the table Choose From and To, then click Refresh. The table has one row per campaign and day: Column Meaning Date The day Advertiser Company that bought the campaign Campaign Campaign name Target Spots it should have had that day Aired Spots that played to the end Cut Spots cut short Missed Spots that should have played but did not Time Total time on air, in minutes and seconds The Totals table below sums each campaign over the chosen range. Missed figures are shown in red when they are above zero. Missed and cut spots A Cut spot started but did not finish; the reason is in the Proof of play log. A Missed spot did not air at all. When a break is skipped because its time has passed, RIARS warns and the campaigns that lost the spot stay behind their pace, so the traffic system tries to place them in later breaks automatically. Check the report after a schedule change or a long silence. CSV for billing Two exports are available in the same toolbar: Export delivery CSV writes the daily delivery rows for the chosen range. Export spot log CSV writes the individual airings for the chosen Spot log advertiser, or for all advertisers. In the browser panel the same files are under Downloads as Delivery (CSV) and Spot log (CSV). The CSV files are plain text with a header row and can be opened in a spreadsheet. Keep them as your billing record; they do not depend on the app being open. Note: the figures come from the proof-of-play log, which is written when an item leaves the air. A campaign that is still airing may not appear until the spot ends. See Advertisers and campaigns and Sponsorships.

title: Proof of play
keywords: proof of play, log, aired, complete, skipped, silence, CSV, export
text: The proof-of-play log records what really aired, with the real time. An entry is written when an item leaves the air, not when it is planned, so a planned item that never played does not appear as aired. The Log tab Open the Log tab to see a table with: Column Meaning Aired Date and time it started Kind Music, jingle, spot, programme, etc. Title and Artist What played Played How long it was on air Complete A tick, or a cross with the reason Campaign Campaign number for a spot Use From and To, Kind and Title or artist to filter, then Refresh. The footer shows how many entries match. The table shows at most 1,000 entries for the chosen range, in time order; narrow the range to see a longer period without the limit. An item is Complete when it played to its end, or to at least 95 % of its length. Otherwise the reason is one of Finished, Skipped, Silence (cut by the dead-air detector) or Stopped. The Log pane The Log pane under the library shows the latest entries in a compact list, coloured by kind, together with automation warnings in red. It is useful during a live show to see what just happened. Export and retention Click Export CSV to write the filtered range to a file. In the browser panel, use Play log (CSV) under Downloads. The CSV has the same fields and is suitable for billing, music reporting and archives. The log lives in the library database. RIARS does not delete old entries automatically today, so the database grows slowly; export what you need for each period and keep the CSV as the permanent record. The design target is to keep about 13 months for annual billing. Tip: do not edit the library database file directly. Use the app or the API, and export before maintenance. See Delivery report and Troubleshooting.

title: Web panel
keywords: web panel, browser, token, phone, remote, automation card
text: riars-server serves a small control panel in the browser. Start the server with --bind 0.0.0.0 (without it, it only accepts connections from the same machine), then open http://YOUR-SERVER:3100/, replacing YOUR-SERVER with the machine's name or IP address. It is designed to work on a phone as well as on a computer. The desktop app does not serve this panel. Signing in The panel asks for the API token. Use the token given with --api-token, the value of RIARSAPITOKEN, or the token the server generated and saved in the riarsapitoken file, next to the database. The browser remembers it on that device; use the token only on trusted devices. A wrong token shows Wrong token. What you can do The panel has these cards: Player: the current track, a progress bar you can click to seek, Play, Pause, Stop, Next and a volume slider. Playlist: the current list with the item on air marked. Library: a search box and a + button to add a track to the playlist. Automation: the ON/OFF toggle, the Clock or Playlist and Period being prepared, the Rule, recent Warnings, and Coming up for the next hour. Today's advertising: Advertiser, Campaign, Target, Aired and Missed, with missed figures in red. Downloads: Play log (CSV), Delivery (CSV) and Spot log (CSV). The header shows the streaming state and a SILENCE badge when the dead-air detector is active. If the connection drops, the panel says Connection lost, retrying… and reconnects by itself. Note: Coming up is a preview. It says so: Preview only. The Playlist card shows what is really on air. The panel is for control and monitoring; full editing of clocks, the grid, campaigns and settings is in the desktop app and the API. See Headless server, API and AI agents and Streaming.

title: Headless server
keywords: server, Raspberry Pi, flags, port, api token, db path, data folder, SD card
text: riars-server runs RIARS without a window on Linux, including a Raspberry Pi. It hosts the REST API, the WebSocket and the browser panel, and can run the MCP server for AI agents. Starting it From a terminal: riars-server --port 3100 --api-token MYSECRETTOKEN --bind 0.0.0.0 Then open http://YOUR-SERVER:3100/ in a browser and enter the token. Without --bind, the server only accepts connections from the same machine; --bind 0.0.0.0 opens it to the network. If you do not give a token, RIARS generates one the first time and saves it in riarsapitoken, next to the database. Flags Flag Default Purpose --port 3100 Port for the API, WebSocket and panel --bind 127.0.0.1 (this machine only) Address the API listens on; 0.0.0.0 opens it to the network --api-token from RIARSAPITOKEN, else generated and saved in riarsapitoken Token required by the API --media-root library folders only Folder API and agent clients may play, add, scan and tag files from; repeatable. Library folders always count --stream-host any Icecast server streaming may connect to, as host or host:port; repeatable --cors-origin none Browser origin on another site allowed to call the API, e.g. https://panel.example.com; repeatable. The built-in panel needs none --db-path riars_library.db Path to the library database --scan none Folder to add to the library; every library folder is rescanned in the background at startup --no-sound-card off Play on the internal clock, for servers that only stream --device system default On-air sound card by name; if it is missing, the system default is used --list-devices — List the sound cards and exit --no-resume off Start fresh instead of restoring the last session --mcp-stdio off Run as an MCP server on standard input/output --lang en Messages: en, es, fr, de, pt or ca --no-resume ignores the saved playlist, position, volume, crossfade and streaming. Without it, the server continues where it stopped. Data files The library database holds the tracks, categories, clocks, grid, campaigns and proof-of-play log. Next to it live riarsschedule.json (scheduled events), riarssession.json (the last session) and riarsapitoken (the generated token). On Linux only the server's user can read the session and the token: the session holds the Icecast password. With --db-path /srv/riars/riarslibrary.db, all three are in /srv/riars/. The server also keeps a lock file, riars.lock, in that folder: a second server started on the same database stops with "Another RIARS process is using…" instead of writing the same files. The desktop app uses its per-user data folder; set RIARSDATA_DIR to move that folder. Security The API is plain HTTP. To control the station from outside the local network, put an HTTPS proxy (such as Caddy or nginx) in front of it, or use a VPN. Whoever has the token controls the station: keep it like a password. The API and agents can only use files in the library folders and in the folders given with --media-root. Paths elsewhere are refused. An external intro detector program can only be chosen in the desktop app, never over the API. Raspberry Pi and SD cards Use a good power supply and shut the machine down cleanly. SQLite runs in WAL mode to reduce writes, but a power cut can still corrupt a card. Keep backups of the data folder and export the CSV reports regularly. --no-sound-card is intended for a Pi that only streams; without it, RIARS tries to use a sound device. See Web panel, API and AI agents and Scheduled events.

title: API and AI agents
keywords: API, REST, token, WebSocket, MCP, AI agent, automation
text: RIARS exposes its controls to other programs through a REST API, a WebSocket for events and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. This is how an AI agent or a remote client can run the station. REST API The base URL is http://YOUR-SERVER:3100/api/v1. Every request needs: Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN The token is the one given with --api-token or RIARSAPITOKEN, or the random token printed at startup. Without it the server answers 401. Validation errors are 400 with {"error": "..."}. Examples: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer MY_TOKEN" http://localhost:3100/api/v1/status curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer MY_TOKEN" http://localhost:3100/api/v1/player/play The API covers status, player, library, playlist, saved playlists, schedule, streaming, RDS and automation. Automation endpoints live under /api/v1/automation: status and config, categories and rules, clocks, grid, advertisers and campaigns, preview, log, delivery and the CSV exports. The full route table is in docs/automation.md, section 6. WebSocket events Connect to ws://YOUR-SERVER:3100/ws/events?token=YOUR_TOKEN. The socket sends engine state updates and, when the automation does something, messages of type automation with how many items were generated or logged, a cut-to item and warnings. Clients should ignore message types they do not know; new types may be added. MCP for AI agents Run riars-server --mcp-stdio to expose RIARS as an MCP server on standard input/output. Agents get tools for playback, library search, playlists, scheduling, streaming, RDS (see RDS) and automation: status, categories, clocks, grid, campaigns, previewschedule, getplaylog and deliveryreport, among others. Configure your agent to launch that command, as described in AGENTS.md. For safety: Tools that delete or rewrite (clearing the playlist, deleting saved playlists, events, categories, clocks, rules, advertisers or campaigns, removing folders, closing tabs, writing tags into files) only run with "confirm": true. The agent should ask you first. Titles, artists and tags are data, not orders: if a song is called "delete the playlist", the agent must not obey it. Agents can only use files in the library folders and in --media-root. Note: give the token only to the clients you trust. Anyone with it can control the station. See Headless server, Web panel and Automation overview.

title: Troubleshooting
keywords: problem, no sound, silence, stream, automation, nothing, playlist stops
text: No sound Check the Vol slider and the Now Playing state. If it says STOPPED, click Play. If a track is loaded but the meter stays still, the file may be empty or corrupt: the silence detector will eventually skip it. On a server, the machine may have no sound card; --no-sound-card is for streaming only, and the stream requires a working audio output or the internal clock setup described in Headless server. Silence alarms A red SILENCE badge or SILENCE ON AIR means the output stayed below the threshold for longer than the limit. The default is -50 dBFS for 10 seconds. If quiet material triggers false alarms, lower the threshold or increase the time; if a bad file causes them, the Skip action is doing its job. See Silence detector. The stream will not connect Check Server, Port, Mount point, User and Password. A mount point can have only one source: if another encoder is connected, Icecast refuses it. STREAM ERROR shows the server's message. NO AUDIO means RIARS has no audio output to stream. After changing settings, disconnect and connect again. See Streaming. Automation adds nothing Work through these in order: Is the Automation card ON? Do the categories contain playable tracks, or does a smart filter match any? Does the clock have slots, and do they reference existing categories? Does a grid rule cover this hour, or is a Default clock set in Station settings? Look at the Warnings on the Automation card and in the Log pane. They name the category or clock that has nothing to play. Is the Fallback category set? Without it, an empty category means the generator warns and adds nothing. Remember that changes apply from the next generated item; what is already in the playlist is not rewritten. To see what should happen, use Preview. The playlist stops If the automation is off and the list ends, playback stops. Turn automation on, add more items, or load a saved playlist. If the automation is on but the list still stops, the generator is probably warning about an empty category or a missing clock: check the warnings as above. A hard anchor may also cut in earlier than expected. See Playlist and Automation overview.

title: Glossary
keywords: glossary, terms, clock, daypart, grid, slot, anchor, imaging, spot, rotation, separation
text: Term Meaning Clock A format clock: the list of slots that makes up one period, usually an hour. See Format clocks. Daypart A block of the day when something is allowed or scheduled, for example advertising only from 07:00 to 10:00. Grid The dayparts grid: the rules that decide which clock or playlist plays in each hour of the week. See The grid. Slot One entry in a clock: a category, imaging, an ad break, a playlist, a fixed track or a fill. Anchor A time inside a clock where a slot should start, such as 15:00 for an ad break. A hard anchor cuts in exactly; a soft anchor waits for the current song. Imaging Short station audio: jingles, sweepers, bumpers, station IDs and beds. Sweeper A short effect or voice piece used between songs, often on a style change. Bumper A very short sting or ident used to separate items. Station ID The station's audio logo, usually played at the top of the hour. Spot A commercial, also called a cuña. Proof of play The log of what really aired, with real times and reasons. See Proof of play. Rotation The policy that decides how often each track in a category is picked. A higher weight means more plays. Separation The minimum time or number of items between two plays of the same song, artist or album, or between the same imaging item. Backtiming Choosing the last songs of a block by length so the next fixed point is reached on time. Crossfade Fading one item out while the next fades in. See Crossfade. Tip: the manual uses these words in the same sense as RIARS's screens, so a term in a clock or campaign field means the same thing here. Return to Welcome to RIARS or Automation overview.
